Hunger
HUNG-ger
v.
Old English hungrian, from hungor (hunger). Renders the Hebrew rā‘ēb, “to be hungry,” and the Greek peinaō, “to hunger, be hungry,” used both of bodily hunger and of the soul’s longing for God and His righteousness.

📖 Biblical Definition

To hunger, in Scripture, is to feel the urgent inward emptiness that craves to be filled—most literally of the body’s need for food, but transferred by the Spirit’s use to the soul’s deep need for God Himself, His Word, and His righteousness. The Beatitude is the verb’s charter: Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled. The blessedness lies precisely in the hunger; the unhungry soul is not commended; the satisfied-with-self soul receives nothing because it craves nothing. Christ in the wilderness, after forty days, was an hungered—and met the tempter with the deeper word: man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God. The saint’s hunger is therefore a moral and spiritual organ. He hungers after Christ as the bread of life; he hungers for the Word as the necessary daily food; he hungers for righteousness as the famished man hungers for bread, with the energy of need; he hungers for the day when his Lord shall return and he shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more, for the Lamb shall feed him and lead him to living fountains of waters. The biblical contrast is sharp: the Laodicean church says I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing, and Christ counsels her to buy of Him gold tried in the fire—the rebuke is that she has lost hunger. The Spirit’s ordinary work in awakening a soul is the awakening of holy hunger; the absence of hunger is the most ominous spiritual symptom; the presence of even small hunger is the most hopeful spiritual sign, because the promise stands: they shall be filled.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HUNGER as an uneasy sensation occasioned by the want of food; a craving of food by the stomach; figuratively, any strong or eager desire.

expand to see more

HUNGER, v.i. — 1. To feel the pain or uneasiness which is occasioned by long abstinence from food. 2. To desire with great eagerness; to long for. Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness (Matt 5:6).

HUNGER, n. — 1. An uneasy sensation occasioned by the want of food. 2. Any strong or eager desire.

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 5:6 — "Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled."

Matthew 4:4 — "But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God."

John 6:35 — "And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst."

Revelation 7:16-17 — "They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more... For the Lamb which is in the midst of the throne shall feed them, and shall lead them unto living fountains of waters."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Spiritual hungering is corrupted by the over-fed satiety of late-modern consumer culture, which has trained the soul to be perpetually filled with lesser things and never to feel the holy emptiness that the gospel addresses—and by the Laodicean self-sufficiency that says I have need of nothing.

expand to see more

Late-modern consumer culture is a discipline in the elimination of hunger. The body is perpetually fed and snacked between meals; the eye is perpetually fed with screens; the ear is perpetually fed with audio; the affections are perpetually fed with entertainment; the appetites are catered to faster than they can form into hunger. The result is a generation whose soul, like its body, has never been allowed to be empty, and which therefore has lost the capacity to feel the deep hunger after God to which the Beatitude promises filling. The believer absorbs the discipline of satiety and brings it to prayer, worship, and the Word with the same dulled appetite he brings to everything else: a soul too well-fed by lesser things to hunger for the better. Recover hunger by removing some of the lesser feedings—the fast, the screen-off, the deliberate spiritual hunger-pang—and the deeper appetites return.

The Laodicean corruption is hunger’s self-flattering twin: the soul that says I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing, and does not realize that it is wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked. The most dangerous spiritual state is not the felt emptiness that drives a soul to Christ but the felt fullness that keeps a soul away. The Beatitude reverses the world’s ranking: blessed are not the satisfied but the hungry, not the filled but the empty, not the rich-in-self but the poor-in-spirit. Where the felt-sufficient cannot be helped, the hungry shall be filled. The recovery is therefore both a discipline (fast from the lesser fillings) and a confession (own the actual emptiness), and the promise stands at the end of both: they shall be filled.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rā‘ēb (to be hungry) and Greek peinaō (to hunger)—both bodily hunger and the soul’s deep craving for God, the Word, the bread of life, and the righteousness that the Beatitude promises shall be filled.

expand to see more

Hebrew rā‘ēb (H7456) — to be hungry, to suffer hunger.

Greek peinaō (G3983) — to hunger, be hungry; used in the Beatitude and of Christ’s wilderness hunger.

Hebrew rā‘āb (H7458) — hunger, famine (the noun).

Greek limos (G3042) — famine, severe hunger.
